newsitem.title: AFGHANISTAN: Government troops hit Taleban north of Kabul.
newsitem.headline: Government troops hit Taleban north of Kabul.

text.p: Forces loyal to ousted government military head Ahmad Shah Masood fought back against Taleban troops on Friday along a vital highway north of Kabul
Reporters who traveled south through the strategic Salang pass met Masood's troops in Olang, and could hear shelling in the distance towards Kabul.
"Taleban hold some parts of the road between here and Kabul and we hold some," said Masood commander Abdul Bashir Salanghi in Olang, just south of the Salang pass.
"There is still fighting in Jabal-os-Saray and Charikar. Perhaps we will take them today or tonight...our troops are fighting and there are some civilians fighting there too."
The pass links the capital Kabul with northern Afghanistan, including territories controlled by the Uzbek warlord Abdul Rashid Dostum.

The fundamentalist Islamic Taleban are suffering the worst military reverses in their two-year existence and have been hit by an accord between Dostum, Masood and Karim Khalilli of the Shia Moslem Hezb-i-Wahadat.

But while Masood's men are fighting in the valley below, trying to regain the initiative against Taleban forces which drove them and the rest of the government out of Kabul two weeks ago, Dostum's soldiers are staying out of the battle.
Masood and Dostum were among a group of anti-Taleban leaders who met north of the Salang pass on Thursday in what some observers billed as a war council.
Dostum's men are taking no part role in the counteroffensive against Taleban, preferring to cement control of the Salang.
Hundreds of Dostum soldiers in winter clothes were guarding all the main ridges along the rugged route and large numbers of tanks, rocket launchers and big guns were dug in along the way.

"If General Dostum gives the order we will attack to the south (along with Masood). For the moment we are holding here," said General Abdul Majid Ruzi, commander of Dostum's troops along the key highway.
Asked how Masood was making so much progess Ruzi said: "The Taleban were so cruel ordinary people have begun to fight."
"This is not just Masood's forces. It is Masood plus citizens," he said.

Taleban forces, who practice an ultra-conservative form of Islam, have imposed strict controls on Kabul, banning women from the workplace, forcing them to wear the veil and insisting men pray in the mosque, rather than at home.
Guerrilla attacks, apparently orchestrated by Masood, have hit the Taleban well behind their front lines.
Village commanders turned on the Taleban, cutting routes north of the capital and fighters loyal to Masood shelled Bagram airbase, 50 km (30 miles) north of Kabul.
Just on from the main pass some 12 km (8 miles) north of Kabul, Taleban militia pounded positions on both sides of the road with rocket, artillery and anti-aircraft fire on Friday.
Fighters said that since morning local commanders in at least four villages had attacked the Taleban. At dusk, several tanks were moving out of the capital towards the fighting.
"Four districts have turned against us," one fighter said.
Afghan-watchers in Kabul said Masood appeared to have reverted to the tactics he used against the Soviet army in the 1980s when Moscow backed a communist Afghan government.
His ethnic Tajiks survived a series of assaults on his Panjsher valley redoubt and often hit back in the Salang Pass. Then they would stage hit-and-run raids in the Soviet rear.
The largely ethnic Pushtun Taleban launched an assault on the gorge that leads into the Panjsher last Saturday. After four days of fighting they had penetrated barely 500 yards (metres).
But Masood's success may depend on the extent of the help he receives from Dostum.

The two charismatic commanders were fighting each other in the Salang earlier this year. With that memory still fresh the Taleban threat has sparked only tacit operation between the two rather than the active alliance some had forecast and hoped for.
